title: The Duplicate Rows

scenario.situation: A Kafka-to-warehouse stream occasionally writes duplicate delivery events, so daily counts are slightly inflated. The lead wants to re-architect the pipeline for exactly-once processing semantics end to end.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The lead believes only true exactly-once streaming semantics will fix the duplicates, and has scoped a large re-architecture to achieve it.
scenario.question: What actually causes the duplicates, and what's the right-sized guarantee to fix them?

decisions.prompt: How do you approach the fix?

options.label: Re-architect the whole pipeline for end-to-end exactly-once
options.detail: Introduce transactional producers, consumers, and sinks across the stack.
options.consequence: You commit to transactional coordination across the stack — one of the hardest guarantees in distributed systems — before even confirming where or how often the duplicates arise.
options.divergenceCost: Committed to the strongest possible guarantee before measuring the actual duplication.

options.label: Quantify the duplicates and trace where they enter the pipeline
options.detail: Measure the duplicate rate and find the mechanism that produces them.
options.consequence: You measure ~0.2% duplicate rows, all appearing after consumer retries following transient failures — at-least-once delivery replaying events the sink already wrote. The duplicates carry a natural key (event_id) and a clear, narrow cause.

options.label: Switch to a different streaming platform said to handle this better
options.detail: Evaluate replatforming the stream onto another system.
options.consequence: You evaluate migrating the whole stream to another platform — a massive change — to sidestep a duplication that a downstream key constraint could absorb.
options.divergenceCost: Considered replatforming to avoid a problem the sink layer can neutralize.

options.label: Add a nightly dedup batch job to clean the table
options.detail: Sweep duplicates out of the warehouse table after the fact.
options.consequence: A nightly cleanup masks the duplicates after the fact, but intra-day counts stay wrong and you've added a second pipeline to babysit — treating the symptom on a delay.
options.divergenceCost: Cleaned up after the duplicates instead of preventing them at write time.

decisions.prompt: You've traced retry-driven duplicates with a natural key. Which approach do you evaluate to fix them?

artifact.title: Two ways to stop duplicate rows

options.label: Full exactly-once semantics across producers, brokers, and consumers
options.detail: Guarantee each event is processed exactly once end to end.
options.consequence: End-to-end exactly-once would eliminate the duplicates — at the cost of transactional coordination across every stage, a large latency and complexity hit, and ongoing operational fragility. It's the maximal guarantee for a minor, well-bounded problem.
options.divergenceCost: Chose the maximal distributed guarantee for a problem confined to the sink write.

options.label: Idempotent upserts on the natural key (event_id) at the sink
options.detail: Make the sink write an insert-or-ignore keyed on event_id so replays are no-ops.
options.consequence: Because every event carries a unique event_id, making the sink write an idempotent upsert makes replays harmless — the second write of the same event is a no-op. This delivers effectively-once results at the sink in a few hours' work, no pipeline-wide transactions, no latency cost.

options.label: Proceed with the exactly-once re-architecture for correctness
options.detail: Deliver the end-to-end guarantee to be sure it never recurs.
options.consequence: You deliver a technically pristine guarantee, but at the price of weeks of high-risk work and a permanently more complex, higher-latency pipeline — to solve a 0.2% duplication a one-line upsert would have erased.
options.divergenceCost: Bought a pipeline-wide guarantee, and its permanent complexity, for a problem the sink could absorb.

options.label: Use idempotent upserts, explain effectively-once vs exactly-once, keep at-least-once delivery
options.detail: Recommend the sink-level fix and the reasoning behind it.
options.consequence: You recommend keeping at-least-once delivery and making the sink idempotent, and explain the distinction: exactly-once delivery is nearly impossible and unnecessary here, while idempotent writes give exactly-once results where it matters — the data. The duplicates vanish, the pipeline stays simple.

insight: The duplicates came from ordinary at-least-once retries replaying events the sink had already written — a narrow, 0.2% problem with a natural key attached. Pursuing end-to-end exactly-once semantics would have rebuilt the entire pipeline with transactional coordination to guarantee something a single idempotent upsert on event_id achieves in hours. The lesson is the distinction between exactly-once delivery (extraordinarily hard, rarely needed) and idempotent, effectively-once results (cheap and usually sufficient): design the sink to make replays harmless and you get correctness where it counts without paying for the strongest guarantee in distributed systems.
